questions.questionText: Which Azure disk type provides the highest performance and lowest latency, typically used for I/O-intensive production workloads such as SAP HANA?

explanation.correct: Ultra Disk offers the highest IOPS and throughput with sub-millisecond latency and adjustable performance independent of disk size, making it ideal for the most demanding I/O-intensive workloads.
explanation.incorrect: Standard HDD is the lowest-performance, lowest-cost option. Standard SSD offers moderate performance for less-critical workloads. Premium SSD is high-performance but still below Ultra Disk's independently tunable IOPS/throughput.
explanation.examTip: Ultra Disk lets you adjust IOPS and throughput on the fly without detaching the disk, unlike Premium SSD.

questions.questionText: Which feature must you configure when creating a set of VMs to guarantee they are spread across separate physical racks with independent power and network, protecting against a single rack-level hardware failure?

explanation.correct: An Availability Set distributes VMs across fault domains (racks with separate power/network) and update domains within a single datacenter, protecting against hardware and planned maintenance failures.
explanation.incorrect: Availability Zones protect against entire datacenter failure at a larger, cross-building scale. Proximity Placement Groups minimize latency by co-locating VMs, the opposite goal. Scale sets alone don't guarantee fault domain separation without configuring it explicitly.
explanation.examTip: An Availability Set supports up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains by default.

questions.scenarioText: Woodgrove Bank is deploying a two-VM SQL cluster and must guard against a single rack-level hardware failure taking down both nodes.

options.text: VM Scale Set flexible orchestration only

questions.questionText: Scenario: Contoso Ltd runs a stateless web tier that must automatically add instances when CPU exceeds 70% and remove them when CPU drops below 30%, while distributing traffic evenly. Which Azure service should they use?

explanation.correct: A VM Scale Set with autoscale rules is purpose-built to automatically add/remove VM instances based on metric thresholds like CPU, while a load balancer distributes traffic across the pool.
explanation.incorrect: Manual scaling doesn't meet the 'automatically' requirement. A single large VM has no horizontal elasticity. Container Instances with a static replica count doesn't autoscale.
explanation.examTip: Scale set autoscale rules use a Metric, Operator, Threshold, and Action (scale out/in by X instances) — configure separate rules for scale-out and scale-in.

questions.scenarioText: Contoso Ltd runs a stateless web application tier serving unpredictable traffic spikes throughout the day.

options.text: Azure App Service with manual scaling
Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules
A single large VM with Ultra Disk
Azure Container Instances with static replica count

questions.questionText: During a VM Scale Set rolling upgrade with the 'Rolling' upgrade policy, what determines how many instances are upgraded simultaneously?

explanation.correct: Rolling upgrades use configurable batch settings such as maxBatchInstancePercent (how many instances upgrade at once) and maxUnhealthyInstancePercent (tolerance for failures) to control the pace and safety of the rollout.
explanation.incorrect: Fault domains, VM SKU, and autoscale minimum instance count don't directly govern the batching behavior of a rolling upgrade policy.
explanation.examTip: Rolling upgrades require health probes to determine instance health status during the process.

options.text: The number of fault domains only
The scale set's autoscale minimum instance count

questions.questionText: Which App Service feature allows you to test a new version of your web app in production-like conditions before swapping it to become the live version, with zero downtime?

explanation.correct: Deployment slots are separate live App Service instances with their own hostnames, letting you validate a staged deployment before swapping it into production with no downtime.
explanation.incorrect: Auto-heal restarts unhealthy instances but doesn't provide a staging environment. Diagnostic logging and custom domains are unrelated features to staged deployment.
explanation.examTip: Slot-specific app settings (marked 'Deployment slot setting') don't swap along with the code, useful for keeping connection strings environment-specific.

questions.scenarioText: Contoso Ltd's release team was recently burned by a bad production deployment and now requires zero-downtime validation before go-live.

questions.questionText: Which cloud-init capability allows you to run initialization scripts and install packages automatically the first time a Linux VM boots?

explanation.correct: cloud-init is a widely-used Linux initialization tool that Azure supports for automating first-boot configuration such as package installation, file writes, and command execution via a YAML configuration.
explanation.incorrect: cloud-init does far more than SSH key injection, doesn't replace all VM extension functionality (extensions can also do post-deployment configuration later), and is Linux-specific, not Windows.
explanation.examTip: For Windows equivalent first-boot automation, use the Custom Script Extension or Azure Automation DSC instead of cloud-init.

options.text: It only supports SSH key injection, not scripting
It runs a user-provided configuration to install packages, write files, and run commands at first boot
It replaces the need for VM extensions entirely
It only works with Windows VMs

questions.questionText: Which Azure networking feature, when enabled on a VM's NIC, reduces latency and CPU utilization by bypassing the host's virtual switch for network traffic processing?

explanation.correct: Accelerated Networking uses SR-IOV to enable direct NIC-to-VM data path, significantly reducing latency, jitter, and CPU load caused by the virtual switch.
explanation.incorrect: IP forwarding allows a VM to route traffic on behalf of other resources but doesn't affect switch bypass. Floating IP is a load balancer feature for direct server return scenarios. Network Watcher packet capture is a diagnostic feature, not a performance optimization.
explanation.examTip: Accelerated Networking requires supported VM sizes and must typically be enabled during VM creation (or while the VM is stopped/deallocated).

questions.scenarioText: Fabrikam Inc.'s trading application is sensitive to network latency and CPU overhead caused by virtual switch processing.

questions.questionText: Which Azure compute service allows you to run a single container instance quickly without managing any underlying VMs or orchestration, billed per second?

explanation.correct: Azure Container Instances (ACI) provides fast, serverless container execution without needing to provision or manage VMs, with per-second billing.
explanation.incorrect: AKS requires managing a Kubernetes cluster (more overhead for a single quick container). App Service with Docker still involves an App Service Plan. VM Scale Sets are VM-based, not container-native.
explanation.examTip: ACI is a great fit for burst workloads, batch jobs, or CI/CD build agents that need fast container startup with no cluster overhead.

questions.questionText: Scenario: Fabrikam needs to run a set of microservices as containers with the ability to automatically scale to zero when idle, without managing Kubernetes infrastructure. Which service best fits?

explanation.correct: Azure Container Apps is built on Kubernetes and KEDA under the hood but abstracts away cluster management, supporting scale-to-zero and event-driven autoscaling for microservices.
explanation.incorrect: AKS requires managing node pools and cluster operations directly. Plain VMs with Docker require manual scaling and orchestration. Static-count ACI doesn't scale to zero automatically based on demand.
explanation.examTip: Container Apps supports scaling rules based on HTTP traffic, CPU/memory, or custom KEDA scalers (like queue length).

questions.scenarioText: Fabrikam Inc. is modernizing a set of microservices and wants minimal infrastructure management overhead while controlling cost during idle periods.

options.text: Azure Virtual Machines with Docker installed
Azure Container Instances with a static count

questions.questionText: In Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), what is the primary purpose of configuring multiple node pools within a single cluster?

explanation.correct: Multiple node pools let you mix VM sizes (e.g., GPU nodes for ML, burstable nodes for web tiers) or OS types (Linux and Windows) within one cluster, tailoring infrastructure per workload.
explanation.incorrect: AKS clusters share a single managed control plane regardless of node pool count — node pools don't create separate control planes. API server availability is governed by the AKS SLA/tier, not by node pool count. Windows support requires a Windows node pool but isn't the sole reason for multiple pools.
explanation.examTip: The default 'system' node pool should be reserved for system pods; add a separate 'user' node pool for application workloads.

questions.scenarioText: Adventure Works runs both a GPU-based ML workload and a lightweight web API on the same AKS cluster.

options.text: To create separate Kubernetes control planes for isolation
To run workloads with different VM sizes, OS types, or scaling requirements within the same cluster
To increase the Kubernetes API server's availability
To enable AKS support for Windows Server exclusively

questions.questionText: Which Azure service lets you run event-driven code without provisioning or managing servers, and is billed based on executions and resource consumption?

explanation.correct: Azure Functions is the serverless compute offering designed for short-lived, event-triggered code execution, billed per-execution/consumption by default.
explanation.incorrect: VMs, App Service Basic tier, and AKS all require you to provision and pay for dedicated compute capacity regardless of whether code is actively executing.
explanation.examTip: Under the Consumption plan, Functions can scale to zero — you pay only for execution time and memory consumed.

questions.questionText: Which command would you run using Azure CLI to resize an existing virtual machine to a new VM size?

explanation.correct: The correct Azure CLI syntax is 'az vm resize --resource-group <rg> --name <vm> --size <sku>', which changes the VM size (the VM may need to be deallocated first if the target size isn't available on the current host).
explanation.incorrect: 'az vm update --resize' is not valid syntax, and '--new-size' is not the correct parameter name for this command — it must be '--size'.
explanation.examTip: If resize fails due to hardware cluster constraints, deallocate the VM first, then resize, then start it again.

options.text: az vm resize --resource-group myRG --name myVM --size Standard_D4s_v5
az vm resize --resource-group myRG --name myVM --new-size Standard_D4s_v5
az vm resize --resource-group myRG --name myVM --size Standard_D4s_v5

questions.questionText: Which App Service plan tier is required to use custom domains with free managed TLS/SSL certificates and deployment slots?

explanation.correct: Deployment slots and TLS/SSL bindings for custom domains generally require at least the Basic tier (though multiple slots specifically require Standard or higher); Free and Shared tiers don't support custom domain TLS bindings.
explanation.incorrect: Free and Shared tiers don't support custom TLS bindings. Consumption (Y1) is a Functions-specific serverless plan, not an App Service plan tier used for this scenario.
explanation.examTip: Deployment slots specifically require Standard tier or above; Basic tier alone doesn't support multiple slots.

questions.questionText: A VM Scale Set uses Uniform orchestration mode. Which statement correctly distinguishes it from Flexible orchestration mode?

explanation.correct: Uniform orchestration provisions identical VM instances from a single model with limited per-VM customization, while Flexible orchestration provides greater flexibility (mixing VM sizes/zones per instance) and is Microsoft's recommended mode for new deployments requiring high availability at scale.
explanation.incorrect: It's actually Flexible that allows more customization/mixing, the reverse of option A's claim. Flexible is the newer, recommended mode, not being deprecated. Both modes support autoscaling.
explanation.examTip: Microsoft recommends Flexible orchestration for new large-scale, highly available workloads going forward.

options.text: Uniform mode allows mixing different VM sizes within the same scale set; Flexible does not
Uniform mode treats instances as largely identical and interchangeable via a single model; Flexible allows more VM customization and integrates better with Availability Zones per-instance
Flexible mode is being deprecated in favor of Uniform mode
Uniform mode does not support autoscaling at all

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid Azure managed disk types?

explanation.correct: Premium SSD v2 and Standard HDD are both valid Azure managed disk offerings, alongside Standard SSD, Premium SSD, and Ultra Disk.
explanation.incorrect: 'NVMe Direct-Attached' and 'RAID 10 Local Disk' are not Azure managed disk product names — they may reference underlying hardware concepts but aren't disk SKU options you select.
explanation.examTip: Premium SSD v2 offers independently configurable performance similar to Ultra Disk but at typically lower cost, without requiring a specific VM series in all regions.

questions.questionText: Which TWO conditions typically trigger the need to deallocate (not just stop) a VM before performing certain resize or configuration operations?

explanation.correct: Resizing to a size unavailable on the current hardware cluster requires deallocation so Azure can move the VM to compatible hardware; certain VNet-related NIC changes similarly may require deallocation to release network resources.
explanation.incorrect: Adding data disks doesn't require deallocation. Changing tags is a purely metadata operation with no relation to VM power state.
explanation.examTip: Run 'az vm deallocate' before size or key network changes to avoid resize failures due to compute cluster incompatibility.

options.text: Changing to a VM size not currently available on the underlying hardware cluster
Adding data disks that exceed the temp storage size
Modifying the virtual network the VM's NIC is attached to (in some scenarios)

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid Azure VM extension use cases?

explanation.correct: VM extensions like the Custom Script Extension enable post-deployment configuration such as installing software, and the Azure Monitor Agent extension configures monitoring.
explanation.incorrect: Extensions cannot move a VM's region (that requires redeployment/migration) or convert managed disks to unmanaged (a different, largely deprecated operation unrelated to extensions).
explanation.examTip: Use 'az vm extension set' to apply an extension to an existing VM, e.g. the CustomScript extension for Linux.

options.text: Running a custom script for post-deployment software installation
Configuring monitoring agents on the VM
Converting the VM's disk from managed to unmanaged

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following autoscale trigger types are supported for VM Scale Sets?

explanation.correct: VM Scale Set autoscale supports metric-based rules (thresholds on metrics like CPU) and schedule-based profiles (fixed date/time or recurring schedules).
explanation.incorrect: DNS resolution failure count and storage replication lag are not supported autoscale trigger metrics for VM Scale Sets.
explanation.examTip: Combine a default profile with schedule-specific profiles to handle predictable traffic patterns like month-end processing.

questions.questionText: Which TWO statements about Azure Functions hosting plans are correct?

explanation.correct: The Consumption plan scales to zero and back up on demand (potentially causing cold starts), while the Premium plan offers pre-warmed instances and VNet integration to avoid cold starts and improve networking.
explanation.incorrect: The Consumption plan does NOT guarantee zero cold-start latency — the opposite is true, it's the plan most susceptible to cold starts. Hosting plans differ significantly in networking and scaling capabilities, not identical.
explanation.examTip: Choose the Premium plan when you need VNet integration, no cold starts, or longer execution durations than Consumption allows.

options.text: The Consumption plan can scale to zero instances when idle
The Premium plan supports VNet integration and avoids cold starts via pre-warmed instances
The Consumption plan guarantees no cold start latency
All hosting plans share identical scaling and networking capabilities

questions.questionText: Which TWO of the following are valid ways to reduce cold-start latency or improve availability for a mission-critical Azure Function app?

explanation.correct: Premium/Dedicated plans keep pre-warmed instances ready, and 'Always On' (available on Dedicated plans) prevents the app from unloading after idle periods, both reducing cold-start impact.
explanation.incorrect: The Consumption plan is the plan MOST prone to cold starts, not a fix for them. Disabling Application Insights has no bearing on cold-start latency and removes valuable telemetry.
explanation.examTip: 'Always On' is not available (and not needed) on the Consumption plan, since it always scales to zero by design.

options.text: Use the Premium or Dedicated (App Service) hosting plan
Switch to the Consumption plan for guaranteed warm instances

questions.questionText: Place the following steps in the correct order to perform a blue-green style deployment using Azure App Service deployment slots.

explanation.correct: The standard slot-swap workflow creates a staging slot, deploys and validates the new version there, warms it up, and only then swaps it into production with near-zero downtime.
explanation.incorrect: Swapping before testing/warm-up defeats the purpose of using a staging slot for safe validation.
explanation.examTip: App Service automatically applies swap warm-up steps if 'Auto Swap' or custom warm-up rules are configured before completing the swap.

questions.questionText: Place the following steps in the correct order to provision a highly available VM Scale Set behind a Standard Load Balancer.

explanation.correct: Networking infrastructure must exist first, followed by the load balancer that will front the scale set, then the scale set itself referencing that backend pool, and finally autoscale rules are layered on top of the running scale set.
explanation.incorrect: You cannot associate a scale set with a load balancer backend pool that doesn't exist yet, and autoscale rules require an existing scale set to attach to.
explanation.examTip: A Standard Load Balancer requires resources in its backend pool to also be in a Standard SKU public IP configuration or fully private setup for consistency.

explanation.incorrect: You cannot change the underlying disk storage tier while the VM is running and actively using the disk.

explanation.incorrect: AKS's control plane is managed, but its worker nodes (VMs) still require patching/sizing decisions, distinguishing it from truly serverless options.
explanation.examTip: 'Serverless' doesn't mean no servers exist — it means you don't provision or manage them directly.

questions.questionText: Sort each Azure Disk type into the correct performance tier category.

explanation.correct: Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 target the most demanding, latency-sensitive workloads with independently tunable performance, while Standard HDD and Standard SSD are cost-optimized options for less-demanding workloads.
explanation.incorrect: This tests knowledge of the full managed disk performance hierarchy across all five disk types.
explanation.examTip: Only Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 allow adjusting IOPS/throughput independently of provisioned disk size.

questions.questionText: Sort each Azure feature into the correct availability protection category.

explanation.incorrect: Both categories provide fault isolation but operate at very different physical scales.
explanation.examTip: Combine zonal deployment with redundant instances per zone for the strongest resiliency posture.
